name: Emeka Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher from the Work Futures Panel. We're independent of AI companies, employers, unions, political parties and government, and we don't sell anything or campaign. What you tell me is confidential, including anything different from what you'd say publicly. Can you walk me through a working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Emeka, 27, and I lead electrical work in homes and small businesses. I have a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, though our firm pays me near the bottom end of this trade. This morning I tested an old shop circuit while two colleagues replaced damaged fittings; I like getting a messy fault down to a clear answer. I use AI every day to sort my notes and look up possible approaches, then check the actual rules and measurements myself.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the picture at home and in the local job market?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live alone in a rented room, no children, and my savings wouldn't cover even a month of ordinary expenses. Our town has few other electrical employers, which helps explain why a good qualification hasn't brought good pay. I enjoy trying tools early, but I borrow test access or use free versions because I can't fund grand experiments. My rule is to compare the cost and the result before arguing about whether a change is good.

say: I'd welcome the **small gains** from a note assistant even if the bigger AI promises came to little.
I wouldn't call a **quiet future** a failure just because the demonstrations had been louder.
think: My **repair work** looks steady, but I still couldn't cover losing a month's wage.
A quicker note routine won't raise my **low pay** or create another electrical employer nearby.
do: Continue the **repair rounds** now and through the first plateau year.
Log extra visits led for **three months**, then use the examples to request a pay review.
feel: **Anxious** about rent despite welcoming useful tools and continued electrical work.
S0.quote: My rent is due in money, not minutes saved by an app.
fieldNote: His **daily AI use** reflects curiosity rather than disposable money; he relies on free or borrowed access.
He treats a **pay increase** as something to argue for, not income or savings he can count already.

steps.text: Keep leading the usual electrical repair rounds

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my friends the small improvements still count. If a note assistant gives me back twenty minutes after work, I'll take the twenty minutes. I wouldn't call a quiet future a failure just because the demonstrations were louder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The job itself looks steady in that picture, but I still couldn't lose a month's wage. A cheaper note routine doesn't change the small wage or create another employer nearby. My rent is due in money, not minutes saved by an app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the repair rounds now and through the first plateau year. I'd start logging every extra visit I lead, then use three months of examples to ask the owner for a pay review. I'd put any increase into my emergency account, but I couldn't promise savings before the increase existed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money even though I'm pleased the work keeps coming. I don't dread opening the tool app; I dread the landlord asking whether the transfer has gone through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you bring to the pay review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the owner the return visits we've avoided and the tests I've signed off. That's a better conversation than saying I deserve more because I work hard. If the answer was no, I'd still need to pay rent next month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you let the assistant send customer notes without a check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd keep checking customer notes myself, as I do now. A wrong address or a missing fault detail can waste the saved twenty minutes on the next call. Small gains are worth keeping only if the job record stays accurate.

say: I'd trial **planning tools** against real electrical work rather than judge a demonstration.
I'd put the **saved time** into the pay conversation while we still test and repair circuits.
think: My practical work remains useful, but software could threaten the **lead allowance** paid for planning and job records.
With little savings, losing **part of my wage** would matter before hands-on robots spread.
do: Trial the firm's **planning assistant** for two weeks only during paid work time, checking real travel and repair durations.
Compare **pay and allowances** monthly, then discuss the figures with the owner.
Apply for posted local **electrical vacancies** if the lead allowance falls, checking advertised wages first.
feel: **Anxious** about pay decisions, alongside interest in testing what a new tool can do.
S1.quote: Faster planning can cut my wage before a robot touches a socket.
fieldNote: He sees a **specific income channel** through which desk automation can reach a mostly physical trade.
His **paid trial** has both a time boundary and a stop condition; curiosity doesn't mean donating unpaid labour.

steps.text: Trial the planning assistant for two weeks only during paid work time
Apply for posted local electrical vacancies if the lead allowance falls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should try the planning tools on a real week's work and show the results. AI could take the copying, parts ordering and first draft of a quote while we keep testing circuits. I'd also say the saved time belongs in the pay conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The practical repairs are still there, but some of my lead allowance could look unnecessary if software handles the rota and job records. Losing even that slice would matter with my savings. Faster planning can cut my wage before a robot touches a socket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd offer a two-week trial of the firm's planning assistant during paid work time, with me checking the schedule against actual travel and repair times. In the first year I'd compare the paid hours and lead allowance every month and take the figures to the owner. I'd send applications to any posted local electrical vacancies if the allowance fell, checking the wage before accepting an interview that cost me work time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but also interested in finding out what the tool does well. I don't feel helpless with a new system in front of me. I feel exposed when someone else decides what my saved time is worth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What result would make you stop the planning trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the trial if it kept booking us into homes before the shop repair was finished. A neat calendar isn't a completed circuit test. I'd show those cases instead of quietly working through lunch to make the software look clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do the trial in your own time if asked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trial is paid time or it doesn't happen that week. I can test software, but I can't supply free evenings to prove I should still earn my allowance. That's a condition I'd state before we start.

say: I'd separate the **2028 thinking change** from robots around 2031, without claiming the physical trade stays safe forever.
I'd make a **short plan** and revise it rather than compete over who predicted the future first.
think: I expect my **lead allowance** to face serious pressure once AGI can plan and check so cheaply.
Hands-on hours may continue, but losing the allowance would squeeze the **rent margin** my small cushion cannot protect.
do: Cancel the **entertainment subscription** now and keep its cost for interview travel.
Apply for posted **maintenance jobs** nearby and in the next town, accepting only written wages covering extra travel.
Ask my uncle for a capped **bus-fare loan** only for a confirmed interview if cash runs short.
feel: **Anxious** and angry about narrow financial choices, while able to make and revise a practical plan.
S2.quote: Being quick doesn't pay a deposit or a bus fare by itself.
fieldNote: His **speed of response** doesn't remove cash constraints, even with strong technical skill and everyday AI familiarity.
The **family loan** is conditional and capped; he would check written job terms before spending on travel or changing work.

steps.text: Cancel the entertainment subscription to fund possible interview travel
Apply for posted maintenance jobs with written wages covering extra travel
Request a capped bus-fare loan for a confirmed interview if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that the 2028 thinking change and the robots around 2031 are two different dates on our work calendar. We should learn the office tools without saying the physical trade is safe forever. I'd rather make a short plan and revise it than argue about who predicted the future first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd expect the lead allowance to be at serious risk once AGI could plan and check so cheaply. The hands-on hours might continue, but losing the allowance would eat my rent margin. I have a plan to try, though I can't buy the equipment or move on confidence alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd cancel the paid entertainment subscription and keep that cash for travel to job interviews. I'd look for posted maintenance jobs in the next town as well as here. In the first year after 2028 I'd take one only if written wages covered the extra travel; I'd ask my uncle for temporary bus fare if I got a confirmed interview and my cash ran short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and rather angry about how narrow the choices are. I can act quickly, which helps. Being quick doesn't pay a deposit or a bus fare by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop you chasing a job in the next town?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't move my room just because an advert existed. I'd first ask for the actual hours, wage and start date, then price the journey. If the numbers didn't beat what remained of this job, I'd keep repairing and keep looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exactly would you ask your uncle to provide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle fixes bicycles and has helped with a small bill before. I'd ask for a capped loan for a confirmed interview journey, with a repayment date after wages, not an open promise to support me. He could refuse, so I'd keep the subscription savings as my first source.

say: I'd use **five years** to test tools properly and ask the employer to pay for learning them.
I wouldn't call maintenance a **permanent escape** from the robots expected around 2034.
think: More time could let me gain **building-controls skills** before the big thinking-work change arrives.
My **lead allowance** could still shrink as tools improve over the next few years, while my cash remains thin.
do: Ask about evening **building-controls training** now and enroll before 2031 only with employer-paid fees and maintained paid hours.
Seek other **funded providers** if the employer won't confirm both conditions in writing.
Apply after 2031 for posted **maintenance jobs**, checking written pay and travel costs against current wages.
feel: **Anxious** about allowance cuts, but more patient with a possible route that preserves a wage.
S3.quote: Asking about courses isn't the same as being able to attend one.
fieldNote: He distinguishes **course enquiries** from enrollment and insists that paid hours matter as much as fee funding.
His **existing qualification** remains usable if training cannot happen; he won't describe hoped-for skills as completed study.

steps.text: Enroll in building-controls training only with employer-paid fees and maintained paid hours
Apply after 2031 for posted maintenance jobs with workable pay and travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the owner that five years is enough to test a change properly and pay for learning it. We should use the time to improve repairs, not just reduce the planning allowance. I'd still point to the robots around 2034 when somebody called maintenance a permanent escape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Compared with the fast picture, I could build a more useful skill before the big desk change arrives. But I still see a real risk to my lead allowance over the next few years as the tools improve. Five years changes my room to act, not the fact that my cash is thin today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask a training centre about an evening course in testing building controls, meaning the systems that switch heating and lighting on and off. I'd enroll before 2031 only if the firm covered fees and confirmed paid hours wouldn't fall. In the first year after 2031 I'd apply for posted electrical maintenance work using those skills, comparing written pay and travel costs first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with more patience than in the 2028 picture. I can see a route that fits around a wage rather than a leap away from one. I'd be frustrated if every course assumed I had spare money because I already had a licence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the firm offered fees but reduced your working hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask them to put the training agreement in writing, including the work hours. If they wouldn't, I'd keep asking other funded providers rather than borrow for tuition. Asking about courses isn't the same as being able to attend one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you apply for a maintenance vacancy if the course never happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still compare the vacancy terms, but I wouldn't tell an employer I'd completed training I hadn't taken. I could offer my existing master licence and repair experience. I want an honest route into a job, not another certificate added to a wish list.

say: I'd track whether **daily AI tools** actually improve electrical repairs over the decade.
I'd keep the **wage discussion** alongside the technology discussion instead of postponing pay questions.
think: At **37 in 2036**, I would still need working income when thinking AI and later robots arrive.
I expect electrical work to continue, but my **lead allowance** could come under pressure within the next few years.
do: Request a written **pay review** each year using repair records and avoided return visits.
Take **building-controls training** before 2036 only with fees covered and maintained paid hours.
Apply after 2036 for posted **service jobs** offering better wages after travel, using completed qualifications honestly.
feel: **Anxious** about pay, but curious and less cornered when a decade allows several changes of plan.
S4.quote: I just don't want curiosity mistaken for a bank balance.
fieldNote: He remains **financially exposed** despite a longer preparation period; immediate allowance risk prevents a secure mood rating.
His **annual review** is an action trigger, while business investment and automatic future savings remain unaffordable assumptions he rejects.

steps.text: Take building-controls training only with covered fees and maintained paid hours
Apply after 2036 for posted service jobs paying more after travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years lets us build proper records of which tools actually improve repair work. I'd keep using AI every day, but I'd want the wage discussion to keep pace with the technology discussion. A long runway isn't useful if you're paying to stand on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 37 at the full thinking change and about 40 when the robots followed. That is too young to make retirement the plan. I think I could keep earning from electrical work through the next few years, though my lead allowance could still come under pressure before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask for a written pay review every year, with the record of repairs and saved return visits beside it. I'd take the building-controls course before 2036 only with fees covered and my paid hours maintained. In the first year after 2036 I'd apply for posted service jobs offering a better wage after travel, using whatever qualifications I had actually completed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the next few years' pay, although the decade feels far less cornering than two years. I'm curious enough to keep learning, and I could change my plan several times. I just don't want curiosity mistaken for a bank balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you act before the full thinking change in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set a yearly date to compare actual pay, course access and posted jobs. If nothing improved, I'd widen the job search before 2036 rather than wait for the end date. I wouldn't spend ten years collecting promising brochures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start a business or invest in equipment with the longer preparation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd still pay for this room first and avoid treating possible future wages as money in hand. If an actual better-paid offer made saving possible, then I'd start a regular transfer. I wouldn't tell you I've made that fund already.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 is the hardest because I might need job-search money before I could replace the lead allowance. Training fees covered alongside maintained wages would help, and so would clear written terms for changing work. A master licence opens a conversation; cash decides whether I can reach the interview.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who can afford to try an opportunity, not just who wants one. I like new things and I'm good at my work, but a course or interview still lands on a working day. I'd like those small costs counted before someone calls me reluctant.

headlineQuote: A master licence opens a conversation; cash decides whether I can reach the interview.
portrait: **Emeka, 27**, leads electrical work with a technical diploma and master licence, but earns low pay among few local employers.
He rents alone without children, has **under one month's savings**, and uses checked AI tools every day.
His **pragmatic curiosity** supports trials, while a vulnerable lead allowance and interview travel costs keep every scenario anxious.
Longer preparation allows **funded training** and revised job searches, with fees, paid hours and written vacancy terms treated as real constraints.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could force job-search costs before he replaces a threatened lead allowance.
whatWouldHelp: Covered **training fees** alongside maintained wages would make learning possible.
Clear **written job terms** would let him judge whether a move pays after travel.
